questions: Which plate is denser, and how can you tell?
What kind of boundary is this?
segments.say: Two plates converge over the ocean. The oceanic plate and the continental plate move towards each other, and the oceanic plate is denser, so it sits lower. Point at the two plates on your student notes diagram before anything bends.

questions: Where exactly does the plate bend?
What is the deep fold called?
segments.say: Too dense to stay afloat, the leading edge of the oceanic plate bends downwards. The deep fold where it dives is the ocean trench. Now try the trench question on your worksheet.

questions: What force drags the rest of the plate down?
What do the earthquakes tell us about the slab?
segments.say: The sinking slab is heavy, so gravity pulls it down and it drags the rest of the plate behind it - slab-pull. As the slab cracks and grinds downwards, earthquakes fire along its path, so the earthquakes map where the slab has reached.

questions: Where does the magma come from?
Why does the volcanic arc run parallel to the trench?
segments.say: Deep down, the slab heats up and releases water that melts the mantle above it. The magma rises through the overriding plate and erupts, building a volcanic arc parallel to the trench. Keep the chain in order as you check your student notes and finish the exit ticket.
segments.watchFor: The continental plate pushes the oceanic plate down underneath it. Listen for students who credit the continental plate with a push. Send them back to scene 3: Nothing pushes it down: the cold, dense slab sinks under its own weight - slab-pull - and drags the rest of the plate behind it.
